title: Non-Arm's Length Relationship - Canadian SR&ED Glossary
description: Understand the tax implications of a Non-Arm's Length Relationship on R&D contracts and costs in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: A non-arm's-length relationship, determined under section 251 of Canada's Income Tax Act, changes how SR&ED claimants treat related-party work. Contract payments to a non-arm's-length performer are excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures; instead, the performer may transfer its qualified expenditures using Form T1146, and non-arm's-length purchases are limited to the supplier's actual cost.

body.text: A non-arm's-length relationship, determined under section 251 of Canada's Income Tax Act, changes how SR&ED claimants treat related-party work. Contract payments to a non-arm's-length performer are excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures; instead, the performer may transfer its qualified expenditures using Form T1146, and non-arm's-length purchases are limited to the supplier's actual cost.

Canada's research and development (R&D) tax incentive architecture—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program under Sections 37 and 127 of the Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) and Part XXIX (Section 2900) of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945)—has undergone its most consequential statutory overhaul in more than a decade1. Enacted into law when Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1) received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the modernized federal regime applies to taxation years beginning after December 15, 20243. The legislative package doubles the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million (increasing the maximum annual federal cash refund from $1.05 million to $2.1 million), widens the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extends the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out test, and restores the eligibility of depreciable capital property (including Shared-Use Equipment) and equipment lease expenditures acquired or incurred after December 15, 20241. Complementing these statutory amendments, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process on April 1, 2026 (via Form T1322), while Federal Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) has proposed a further $930 million five-year expansion to bring initial regulatory certification testing and intellectual property (IP) patent and software registration and maintenance costs into the SR&ED base for taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 20263.

First, the notional overhead rate under the Proxy Method (Income Tax Regulations subsection 2900(4)) is strictly 55% of the eligible salary base—not 65% (which last applied in 2012) or 60% (which applied only in 2013)4. Second, contrary to secondary commentary suggesting that Bill C-15 restored purchased capital equipment while leaving leased equipment excluded15, the CRA's official SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026) and updated Form T661 (Version 26) (Lines 350 and 355) confirm that equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 are once again allowable SR&ED expenditures (at 100% if used all or substantially all [90% or more] for SR&ED, or at 50% under the Proxy Method if used primarily [more than 50% and less than 90%] for SR&ED)1. Third, for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished eight legacy R&D tax measures—including the former R&D Salary Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.7, which paid 14% to 30%)—and replaced them with the single refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Form RD-1029.8.CR), which pays 30% on the first $1 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures (including capital equipment) above an exclusion threshold, and 20% on the excess18. Fourth, reductions to the SR&ED expenditure pool and qualified expenditures for government and non-government assistance are governed by paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(11.1) and 127(18) of the Income Tax Act—not subsection 37(2), which governs SR&ED carried on outside Canada4.

body.text: 1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The legal foundation for all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada resides in the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (ITA), which generally conforms to the international OECD Frascati Manual standard3. This statutory definition was left untouched by Bill C-1537. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and that falls into one of three primary categories, supplemented by a fourth category of eligible support work and bounded by seven explicit statutory exclusions30:

items: Basic Research (paragraph 248(1)(a)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view30. While traditionally concentrated in universities, government laboratories, and non-profit research institutes, basic research is also conducted by commercial enterprises in sectors such as biotechnology, nanotechnology, computer applications, and advanced materials30.

Applied Research (paragraph 248(1)(b)): Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view30. Applied research shares the practical orientation of experimental development while seeking to expand the underlying scientific knowledge base30.

Experimental Development (paragraph 248(1)(c)): Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto18. Experimental development is the most commonly claimed category of corporate SR&ED in Canada30.

Support Work (paragraph 248(1)(d)): Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to only the following eight exhaustive statutory categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research3.

body.text: Support work is not SR&ED in isolation22. Under paragraph 248(1)(d), work in these eight categories qualifies only where it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research (paragraph (a)), applied research (paragraph (b)), or experimental development (paragraph (c)) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer3. While paragraph 248(1)(g) excludes research in the social sciences or the humanities (including management science), paragraph 248(1)(d) specifically permits psychological research when undertaken directly in support of eligible core SR&ED30.
Statutory Exclusions: Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)
Even where a project involves genuine core SR&ED, paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k) of the Income Tax Act expressly exclude seven categories of activity from the definition of SR&ED30:

items: Paragraph 248(1)(e): Market research or sales promotion30;
Paragraph 248(1)(f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes30;
Paragraph 248(1)(g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities30;
Paragraph 248(1)(h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas30;
Paragraph 248(1)(i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process30;
Paragraph 248(1)(j): Style changes30; and
Paragraph 248(1)(k): Routine data collection30.

body.text: As the CRA clarifies in its administrative guidance, the critical dividing line between eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as data collection or testing) and excluded work under paragraphs (f) or (k) is purpose30. If data collection or testing is performed to support normal commercial operations or routine quality assurance, it is excluded; if it is carried out specifically and exclusively to test a hypothesis and resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty within an active SR&ED investigation, it qualifies as support work30. Furthermore, conducting excluded activities (such as mineral prospecting) alongside eligible SR&ED does not taint the eligible SR&ED work, provided the excluded activities are carved out of the claim30.
1.2 The CRA's Two-Pillar Eligibility Framework: The "Why" and the "How"

On August 13, 2021, the CRA replaced its archived Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (which had structured administrative reviews around five explicit questions) with the current Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives30. The current guidelines distil the statutory text of subsection 248(1) into two mandatory, cumulative requirements that every project must satisfy3:

The first pillar is The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty). Under this requirement, work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement3. Specifically, the work must seek to generate or discover conceptual knowledge (such as new theories, principles, or predictive models that advance the understanding of science or technology) rather than merely collecting factual knowledge (such as routine measurements or parameters)30. New scientific or technological knowledge is required only when a scientific or technological uncertainty exists—that is, when it cannot be determined in advance whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, because the available scientific or technological knowledge (defined as the combined knowledge of the resources within the claimant's business plus all knowledge reasonably available publicly) is insufficient3.

The CRA recognises several objective indicators that available technological knowledge is insufficient, including situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, specifications do not conform to established standards, parameters fall outside normal operating ranges, too many interdependent variables or unknowns interact (system uncertainty), data is not readily available, or interlocking constraints prevent standard engineering trade-offs30. Cost targets alone do not create technological uncertainty, though attempting to achieve technical performance within strict cost constraints can impose a technological uncertainty30. If a technical team encounters a technological uncertainty and circumvents it using a known workaround, or acquires the solution by hiring a consultant, purchasing proprietary know-how, or completing off-the-shelf training, no technological advancement is achieved and the work is ineligible30. Conversely, if the team systematically investigates the uncertainty to generate new technological knowledge, the "Why" requirement is met even if the experiment fails or the resulting prototype is commercially unsuccessful3.

The second pillar is The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search). Following a systematic approach, standard engineering protocol, or agile software development methodology to build a product is not sufficient30. The work must be carried out as a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis3. Under the CRA guidelines and controlling case law, this requires four sequential elements3:

items: Defining the scientific or technological problem or uncertainty and generating an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for investigation (formulating a hypothesis)3;
Testing the hypothesis by means of planned experiments or rigorous mathematical or engineering analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve iteratively as test data is observed)3;
Developing logical conclusions based on the empirical results or analytical findings3; and
Keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses3.

body.text: 1.3 Dual-Benefit Mechanics: Section 37 Deduction Pool vs. Section 127 Investment Tax Credit

A foundational principle of Canadian R&D tax auditing is that the federal SR&ED program delivers two distinct, sequential statutory benefits that must never be conflated in working papers3. First, The Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures is a running, cumulative tax deduction pool computed under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act3. A taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct any portion of a positive Section 37 pool balance in computing net business income for the current taxation year, or carry the undeducted balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years23. Second, The Section 127 SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (ITC) is an annual tax credit computed under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) (and refunded under section 127.1) on the taxpayer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year5. Unlike the Section 37 deduction pool, the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool is calculated strictly on an annual basis and does not carry over from year to year; rather, the resulting unclaimed ITCs are either refunded in cash, applied against Part I tax payable, carried back 3 taxation years, or carried forward 20 taxation years4.
Additions and Reductions to the Section 37 Deductible Pool

Under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, the running balance of the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool is determined by the statutory additions in paragraphs 37(1)(a) through (c.3) minus the statutory reductions in paragraphs 37(1)(d) through (h)23:

cells: Current expenditures made in the year on SR&ED carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by the taxpayer and related to a business of the taxpayer (includes 100% of direct SR&ED salaries, materials consumed/transformed, post-Dec 15, 2024 equipment leases, and Traditional Method overhead)22.

Current expenditures made in the year for SR&ED carried on in Canada directly undertaken on behalf of the taxpayer (arm's-length and non-arm's-length SR&ED contracts). Included at 100% in the Section 37 deduction pool (unlike the 80% inclusion for Section 127 ITCs)22.

Third-party payments to a corporation resident in Canada (A Entity) to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the taxpayer, where the taxpayer is entitled to exploit the results (included at 100% in the Section 37 pool in the year the SR&ED is performed)22.

Restored Capital Expenditures: Expenditures of a capital nature made on SR&ED carried on in Canada in respect of depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (excluding land, leasehold interests in land, and buildings other than prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903), subject to the available-for-use rule in subsection 37(1.2). Under subsection 37(6), any amount deducted under 37(1) in respect of capital property is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed under paragraph 20(1)(a)1.

body.text: Crucial Tax Interactions: Paragraphs 12(1)(v), 12(1)(t), and Subsection 37(4)

When reductions to the Section 37 pool (most commonly the prior-year federal SR&ED ITC reduction under paragraph 37(1)(e) or current-year provincial assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d)) exceed the opening pool balance plus current-year pool additions—which frequently happens when a claimant elects the Proxy Method and deducts its entire Section 37 pool each year, since the PPA generates an ITC that reduces the pool in the following year even though the PPA itself was never added to the pool—the resulting negative balance must be included in computing the taxpayer's business income for the year under paragraph 12(1)(v)14. That paragraph 12(1)(v) inclusion is then added back to the Section 37 pool in the subsequent year under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) to restore the pool to zero23.

Similarly, federal SR&ED ITCs applied against Part I tax or refunded in cash in Year 1 reduce the Section 37 pool in Year 2 under paragraph 37(1)(e) (or, in the case of Shared-Use Equipment ITCs, reduce the Undepreciated Capital Cost [UCC] of the CCA class in Year 2)23. To the extent that a tax basis reduction under paragraph 37(1)(e) or UCC does not occur, paragraph 12(1)(t) requires the amount of the ITC claimed or refunded to be included directly in the taxpayer's taxable income in the following taxation year15. Furthermore, the portion of a provincial R&D tax credit that relates to the notional PPA reduces federal qualified expenditures and is included in taxable income on Schedule 1 in the year received16.

Under subsection 37(4), no deduction may be made under subsection 37(1) in respect of an expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (such as purchasing a patent, software copyright, or technology licence from another party)28. Only the performer who undertook the SR&ED is entitled to the tax incentives28. Finally, under subsection 37(2), current expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada (directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer and related to the taxpayer's business) are deductible in computing business income in the year incurred, but they do not enter the subsection 37(1) pool and do not earn Section 127 ITCs4. Permissible salary or wages paid to employees performing SR&ED outside Canada may be included on Form T661 (Line 265) under the rules in Section 10.0 of the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, whereas all other foreign R&D expenses are deducted as ordinary business expenses46.
2. Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, Caps and Refundability
2.1 Basic (15%) and Enhanced (35%) ITC Rates

Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), eligible claimants earn an SR&ED ITC at one of two federal rates5. The Basic ITC Rate of 15% is available to all eligible claimants—including corporations (foreign-controlled corporations, large public corporations, and CCPCs or ECPCs on expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit), individuals (sole proprietorships), partners of a partnership, and beneficiaries of certain trusts—on their SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year5. The Enhanced ITC Rate of 35%—comprising the 15% basic rate plus a 20% statutory enhancement—is available to qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit5.
2.2 The $6 Million Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Mechanics (Bill C-15)

Enacted by Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, and effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual Expenditure Limit under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) doubled from $3,000,000 to $6,000,0004. At the 35% enhanced rate, a qualifying CCPC or ECPC can now earn up to $2,100,000 per year in enhanced ITCs (up from $1,050,000 under the pre-December 16, 2024 rules)4. Qualified expenditures in excess of the corporation's expenditure limit automatically earn the 15% basic rate6.
CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Tax Years Beginning After December 15, 2024)

For a CCPC (and its associated corporations), the $6,000,000 baseline expenditure limit phases out linearly under subsection 127(10.2) based on the taxable capital employed in Canada (reported on federal Schedule T2SCH33, T2SCH34, or T2SCH35) of the corporation and its associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year5. Under Bill C-15, the taxable capital phase-out range expanded from $10 million–$50 million (for tax years beginning before December 16, 2024) to $15 million–$75 million (for tax years beginning after December 15, 2024)3. Expressed mathematically, for a full 365-day taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024, the CCPC's annual expenditure limit is5:

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (combined with that of associated corporations) is $15,000,000 or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

Equivalently, for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada above $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $1 across the $60,000,000 phase-out band from $15,000,000 to $75,000,000, reaching nil ($0) once prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,0005. If the corporation has a short taxation year, the expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 3655.
Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the 3-Year Revenue Phase-Out

A major structural reform of Bill C-15 is the extension of the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 20243. Under subsection 127(9), a corporation qualifies as an ECPC throughout a taxation year if it satisfies three statutory conditions: (1) it is resident in Canada; (2) it is a public corporation listed on a designated stock exchange; and (3) it is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons (determined under the statutory assumption that if all shares owned by non-residents were owned by a single particular person, the corporation would still not be controlled by that person)5.

Under subsection 127(10.6), an ECPC's $6,000,000 maximum expenditure limit phases out linearly based on the corporation's average annual gross revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years (as reflected in the financial statements of the corporation or, if part of a consolidated group, the consolidated financial statements of the group) between $15,000,000 and $75,000,0004. If an ECPC has fewer than three preceding fiscal years, the average is calculated using its actual number of preceding fiscal years5. Where an ECPC is a member of a consolidated group, the expenditure limit must be shared and allocated among the group members on a prescribed form; failure to file the allocation agreement results in the CRA determining the ECPC's expenditure limit to be nil5.
Elective 3-Year Revenue Test for CCPCs (Subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32))

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a standalone CCPC (subsection 127(10.31)) or a group of associated CCPCs (subsection 127(10.32)) may formally elect on a prescribed form to compute its $6,000,000 expenditure limit phase-out using the ECPC 3-year average annual gross revenue test ($15M to $75M) instead of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada4. This election benefits capital-intensive private corporations that have raised over $15 million to $75 million in equity or debt financing (which increases taxable capital) while remaining pre-revenue or generating less than $15 million in three-year average gross revenue4. If a CCPC is associated with other CCPCs, all associated CCPCs in the group must jointly elect to use the revenue method, and the group's three-year average revenue must aggregate the financial statement revenues of every member of the group over the preceding three fiscal years regardless of whether they were associated throughout that entire three-year period5.
Associated Corporations and Allocation Rules (Subsections 127(10.3), 127(10.4), and Section 256)

Associated CCPCs (as defined under subsections 256(1) to (5.1) of the Income Tax Act and reported on Schedule 9, Related and Associated Corporations) must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit across the entire associated corporate group4. The group must file Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) to allocate the available expenditure limit among the associated members5. Under subsection 127(10.4), if any member of the associated group fails to file the allocation agreement within 30 days of a written request by the CRA, the CRA may allocate the expenditure limit among the corporations or set it to nil5.
2.3 Complete Refundability Matrix by Claimant and Expenditure Type

Under section 127.1 and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, an SR&ED ITC must first be applied under subsection 127(5) to reduce the taxpayer's Part I federal income tax otherwise payable for the current taxation year to nil5. Any remaining unclaimed balance of the ITC earned in the current year may be refunded in cash according to the claimant's legal classification and whether the expenditure is of a current nature (including the PPA) or a capital nature5. Under subsection 127.1(3), any ITC refunded to the taxpayer is deemed to have been deducted under subsection 127(5), thereby preventing the refunded credit from being carried back or carried forward and triggering the subsequent-year pool reduction under paragraph 37(1)(e)5.

body.text: Qualifying Corporation vs. General CCPC Refundability Rules

A critical subtlety in Section 127.1 is the distinction between a general CCPC and a Qualifying Corporation (subsection 127.1(2))5. Any CCPC (other than an excluded corporation) receives 100% refundability on the 35% enhanced ITC earned on current expenditures and PPA (and 40% refundability on capital expenditures) up to its Expenditure Limit regardless of its prior-year taxable income5. However, to receive a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on expenditures above the Expenditure Limit, the CCPC must also qualify as a Qualifying Corporation5. A CCPC is a Qualifying Corporation if its taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year (combined with the taxable incomes of all associated corporations for their last taxation year ending in the preceding calendar year) did not exceed its Qualifying Income Limit6.
Under the post-December 15, 2024 rules enacted by Bill C-15, the Qualifying Income Limit formula is updated to align with the $15M–$75M taxable capital phase-out6:

where A is $0 if the combined prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated corporations does not exceed $15,000,000, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,0006. (For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the formula used $40,000,000 and a $10,000,000 threshold6.)
2.4 Partnerships, Trusts, Carryovers and Loss Restriction Events

Because a partnership is not a "person" under the Income Tax Act, the CRA's SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy and subsection 127(8) establish that a partnership cannot claim an ITC or hold a multi-year Section 37 pool in its own right6. Instead, the partnership deducts current-year SR&ED expenditures in computing partnership net income for the fiscal period, and calculates a partnership ITC at a fixed 15% rate (even if all partners are CCPCs; partnerships cannot access the 35% enhanced rate, nor can they utilize non-arm's-length expenditure transfers)6.

Under the partnership allocation rules, no SR&ED ITC may be allocated to a "specified member" of the partnership (which includes any limited partner and any passive general partner)6. Unallocated ITCs attributable to specified members are reallocated to the non-specified (active general) partners in a reasonable proportion based on their investment, including partnership debt obligations6. An active general partner receiving reallocated ITCs may elect on Form T932 (Election by a Member of a Partnership to Renounce Investment Tax Credits Pursuant to Subsection 127(8.4)) to renounce all or part of those reallocated credits so that the partnership's deductible SR&ED expenditure pool is not reduced by the renounced ITC in the same fiscal period6. Furthermore, any partnership loss created or increased by deducting SR&ED expenditures is disallowed to a limited partner (the limited partner's deductible loss is reduced by the lesser of the SR&ED deduction and the total partnership loss)6. For trusts, only graduated rate estates and communal organizations (deemed inter vivos trusts under section 143) can designate an SR&ED ITC to their beneficiaries under subsection 127(7)6.

Non-refundable or unrefunded SR&ED ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years (subsection 127(5)) to reduce Part I tax paid in prior years, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years4. When a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (a Loss Restriction Event), its undeducted Section 37 expenditure pool (subsection 37(6.1)) and its unused Section 127 ITC carryforwards are streamed3. They may be carried forward and deducted or claimed in post-acquisition taxation years only if the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related continues to be carried on by the corporation for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of the corporation's income (before making any Section 37 deduction) or Part I tax payable from that same business or a similar business23.
3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
3.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)

When filing Form T661, a claimant must elect in Part 3 between two mutually exclusive calculation methodologies for overhead and indirect expenditures: The Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), elected by ticking Line 160 of Form T661) or The Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A), elected by ticking Line 162 of Form T661)16. The election is made annually for each taxation year and is irrevocable once Form T661 is filed for that year16. If a claimant fails to tick either box on Form T661, the Traditional Method applies by default16. A claimant may switch freely between the Proxy Method in one taxation year and the Traditional Method in the next16.
The 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) (Income Tax Regulations Subsection 2900(4))

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not track or claim actual SR&ED overhead expenditures on Form T66114. Instead, the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of its eligible SR&ED salary base under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations4. The PPA rate was 65% for taxation years ending before 2013, 60% for the 2013 calendar year, and has been fixed at 55% since January 1, 20144. Any calculation or advisory report applying a 65% proxy rate to a 2025 or 2026 claim overstates the notional overhead by 10 percentage points4.

The PPA is a purely notional figure included in the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (Line 502 of Form T661) solely for the purpose of earning federal and provincial SR&ED ITCs3. The PPA cannot be added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool3. Instead, the actual underlying business overhead expenses (utilities, support staff, office supplies, training, etc.) remain ordinary business expenses that may be deducted in the year under subsection 9(1) / paragraph 18(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act in computing net business income14.
The Overall Cap on the PPA (Income Tax Regulations Subsection 2900(6))

Even when 55% of the salary base is properly calculated, subsection 2900(6) of the Income Tax Regulations imposes an Overall Cap on the PPA to ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed the taxpayer's total business deductions for the year2. In Part 5, Section B of Form T661, the PPA cannot exceed the amount determined by the formula A − B − C14:

items: A: Total of all amounts deducted in computing the taxpayer's net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including Cost of Goods Sold)2;

B: Total statutory deductions claimed in the year under sections 20 (e.g., Capital Cost Allowance, interest, bad debts), 24 (ceasing business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (the current-year SR&ED expenditure deduction itself), 66 to 66.8 (resource exploration and development), and 104 (trusts) of the Income Tax Act14; and
C: Any outlay or expense made or incurred in the year for the use of, or the right to use, a building (e.g., commercial office or factory rent) other than a prescribed special-purpose building2.

body.text: As a general rule, the Overall Cap under Regulation 2900(6) will not restrict the 55% PPA so long as the business has deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED, non-building, non-Section 20 operating expenses for every $100 of eligible salary in the proxy base14. Companies whose expenses consist almost entirely of SR&ED salaries (deducted under Section 37 in B) and building rent (deducted in C) are vulnerable to PPA reduction under Regulation 2900(6) and should calculate the cap prior to electing the Proxy Method14.

body.text: 3.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees and Unpaid Remuneration

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means income from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I (Sections 5 to 8 of the Act), including gross T4 base pay, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, and qualifying taxable benefits under Section 655. It strictly excludes dividends, extended vacation or sick leave, retiring allowances, stock option benefits under Section 7, and the employer's share of payroll-related benefits (such as employer CPP, EI, and group benefit contributions)16. While cash-outlay taxable benefits may be included in SR&ED salary or wages, a non-cash taxable benefit (including automobile standby charges and operating expense benefits) is allowable only if: (1) it represents a reasonable estimate of actual costs incurred by the employer; (2) it excludes GST/HST or PST (unless no input tax credit or refund was claimed); and (3) the actual underlying costs (including CCA) are not also deducted as business expenses under Section 955.
Directly Engaged Tasks and the All-or-Substantially-All (ASA) Rule

Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV)), only the portion of salary or wages of employees who are "directly engaged" in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—meaning hands-on technical work, experimentation, analysis, eligible support work, or direct technical supervision of hands-on personnel—may be claimed, based on the proportion of time spent on SR&ED36. Whether an employee is directly engaged in SR&ED is a question of fact based on the tasks performed rather than the employee's job title36. Under Regulation 2900(5) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(IV), if an employee spends all or substantially all (90% or more) of their employment time in the taxation year directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages is deemed to be for SR&ED14.
Specified Employee Restrictions (Subsections 37(9), 37(9.1) and Regulations 2900(7)–(9))

A "specified employee" (subsection 248(1)) is an employee who is a "specified shareholder" of the employer—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or any corporation related to it (counting shares owned by persons with whom the employee does not deal at arm's length)—or an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer (such as a spouse, sibling, or other related individual)16.
The Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose four strict statutory limitations on specified employees14:

items: Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9)): Bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are excluded from allowable SR&ED salary or wages expenditures under both the Traditional and Proxy methods55. (For non-specified employees, bonuses and profit-based pay are allowable in the Section 37 deduction pool and Section 127 direct wage line, though excluded from the Proxy salary base under Regulation 2900(9); additionally, if an employee's sole remuneration in the year consists of bonuses or profit-based pay, the CRA considers an amount commensurate with their direct SR&ED duties to be salary or wages4.)

Deductible SR&ED Wage Cap — 5 × YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1)): The maximum SR&ED salary or wages that can be claimed in the Section 37 pool (Line 305 of Form T661) for a specified employee is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee16. For calendar year 2026, the CPP YMPE is $74,600, so the maximum deductible SR&ED salary for one specified employee for a full 365-day taxation year ending in 2026 is 5 × $74,600 = $373,00016.

Proxy Salary Base Exclusions for All Employees (Regulation 2900(9)): When computing the salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 to which the 55% PPA applies, Regulation 2900(9) excludes—for both specified and non-specified employees—all taxable benefits under Section 6, stock option benefits under Section 7, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and prior-year unpaid wages deemed incurred when paid under subsection 78(4) (Line 310)4.

Proxy Salary Base Cap for Specified Employees — Lesser of 75% and 2.5 × YMPE (Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8)): For each specified employee, the amount of direct SR&ED salary included in the Part 5 proxy salary base cannot exceed the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (after excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages) and 2.5 × YMPE × (Days Employed in the Tax Year ÷ 365)4. With the 2026 YMPE at $74,600, the maximum proxy salary base for one specified employee employed for all 365 days of a taxation year ending in 2026 is 2.5 × $74,600 = $186,50016.

body.text: Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations in taxation years ending in the same calendar year (or deemed associated entities under Regulation 2900(10)), the 5 × YMPE deductible wage cap and the 2.5 × YMPE proxy salary base ceiling must be shared across the associated corporate group14. Under subsections 37(9.2) and 37(9.3), each associated corporation must file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development [SR&ED]) no later than its respective SR&ED reporting deadline; otherwise, the amount claimed for the salary or wages of the specified employee is deemed not to be an expenditure on SR&ED55.

To illustrate these caps in a 2026 claim, consider an owner-manager (specified employee) who earns $200,000 in base salary (with no bonuses or taxable benefits) during a taxation year ending December 31, 2026, and spends 80% of their time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada16. Their direct SR&ED salary is 80% × $200,000 = $160,000, which is below the 2026 subsection 37(9.1) ceiling of $373,000 (5 × $74,600) and is claimed in full on Line 30516. However, for the Part 5 proxy salary base under Regulation 2900(7), the owner-manager's $160,000 direct SR&ED salary is restricted to the lesser of 75% of total salary (75% × $200,000 = $150,000) and 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500), capping the owner-manager's proxy salary base at $150,000 (which generates 55% × $150,000 = $82,500 in PPA)14. Similarly, in an example where a specified employee receives $250,000 in total compensation (including a $30,000 bonus and $10,000 taxable benefit) and spends 90% of their time on SR&ED, stripping the $30,000 bonus and $10,000 benefit leaves $210,000, yielding 90% × $210,000 = $189,000 in deductible SR&ED salary on Line 305, while the proxy salary base is restricted by the 75% rule (75% × $210,000 = $157,500) or the applicable 2.5 × YMPE limit67.
Unpaid Remuneration (Subsection 78(4) — The 180-Day Rule)

Under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, if any salary or wages accrued in a taxation year remain unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of that taxation year, the unpaid amount is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year, but rather in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid (a payment made on the 180th day is considered paid within the limit)55. Claimants must identify unpaid salary or wages not paid within 180 days on Line 315 of Form T661 in the year incurred, and report them on Line 310 of Form T661 in the subsequent year when paid (amounts reported on Line 310 are excluded from the Part 5 proxy salary base under Regulation 2900(9)(b))14. Reasonable vacation or holiday pay and deferred amounts under a salary deferral arrangement are deemed paid on the 180th day (making them deductible in the year, though still excluded from the PPA salary base)55. Under paragraph 18(1)(e), no deduction is allowed for contingent liabilities or reserves; an accrued wage must be a genuine, enforceable legal liability, and timely remittance of payroll source deductions to the CRA is treated as the best evidence of payment55.
3.3 Subcontractors, Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's-Length Contracts and Third-Party Payments

The Income Tax Act and CRA policy draw a sharp legal distinction between SR&ED Contract Expenditures (work performed on behalf of the claimant under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)) and Third-Party Payments (payments to external corporations, universities, research institutes, or consortia to be used for SR&ED under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii))22.

body.text: Critical Subcontracting Rules for Audit Compliance

When a claimant contracts with an arm's-length party to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada, 100% of the eligible current contract expenditure is added to the Section 37 deduction pool, but under paragraph 127(9)(a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" (and paragraph (g)), only 80% of the eligible contract expenditure (and 80% of a third-party payment) is included in Section 127 qualified expenditures for ITC calculation purposes4. Furthermore, an arm's-length current contract expenditure qualifies for the 80% Section 127 ITC inclusion only if it is paid or payable to a "taxable supplier" (subsection 127(9))—meaning a person resident in Canada, a Canadian partnership, or a non-resident person carrying on business through a permanent establishment in Canada22. If a Canadian company contracts out SR&ED to a foreign corporation without a Canadian permanent establishment, the expenditure may enter the Section 37 deduction pool (if performed in Canada), but cannot be included in Section 127 qualified expenditures for ITC purposes49.

If a claimant contracts out only support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) to an arm's-length supplier, the payer can claim 80% of the expenditure provided the work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development performed in Canada by or on behalf of the payer22. The arm's-length performer cannot claim support work on its own because support work in isolation does not meet the definition of SR&ED22. Where an arm's-length performer performs eligible SR&ED for a Canadian payer, the performer's own qualified expenditures are reduced by the "contract payment" received or receivable from the payer under subsection 127(18)4. Under the look-through rule in subsection 37(14) (repealed by Bill C-15 in respect of property acquired on or after December 16, 2024), a payer's SR&ED contract expenditure must be reduced by any amount incurred by the performer that is not an expenditure of a current nature (such as capital property acquired before December 16, 2024), and under subsection 37(15), the performer must inform the payer in writing of that reduction without delay upon request and no later than 90 days after the end of the calendar year22.

For Non-Arm's-Length (NAL) Contracts (determined under section 251), subsection 37(13) deems support work performed by a NAL performer to be SR&ED to the extent that the work would have been SR&ED had it been performed directly by the NAL payer22. Under subsection 127(9) (paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure") and subsection 127(24), contract payments made to a NAL performer are excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures22. Instead, the NAL performer calculates its own qualified expenditures (including its 55% PPA) and may transfer all or part of those qualified expenditures to the NAL payer by jointly filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13)22. Similarly, when materials or capital property are purchased or services are obtained from a NAL party, subsections 127(11.6) to 127(11.8) limit the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to the adjusted selling cost or adjusted service cost actually incurred by the NAL supplier, eliminating any intercompany profit element26. Where government or non-government assistance applies across NAL parties, it may be allocated using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(20)17. Finally, under subsection 127(26), any non-wage SR&ED expenditure that remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which it was incurred is deemed not to be a qualified expenditure for ITC purposes until the taxation year in which it is actually paid (though it still enters the Section 37 deduction pool in the year incurred)22.
3.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and ITC Recapture

Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) (Proxy Method) and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) / Regulation 2900(2)(a) (Traditional Method), a claimant may claim 100% of the laid-down cost (invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, acquisition costs, and storage costs; or production cost including direct labour and production overhead for internally manufactured inventory) of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (Line 320 of Form T661)16.

According to the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), "materials for SR&ED" must be physical and tangible items in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state that compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is carried out or that results from the SR&ED66. Capital property, data, software licences, leases, broken or used lab supplies, cleaning supplies, CDs/DVDs, used lubricants, and general utilities (water, electricity, natural gas) do not qualify as materials for SR&ED66.

Materials Consumed are materials that are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED66. They are claimable only in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed in SR&ED (not when purchased into inventory) and are not subject to ITC recapture unless proceeds received (such as insurance proceeds) exceed 10% of the cost of the materials52. Materials Transformed are materials that are changed or incorporated into another product, prototype, or commercial asset during the prosecution of SR&ED (including input materials forming part of experimental production resulting from experimental development [ED+EP]), where the materials are not destroyed or rendered virtually valueless66.

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if property whose cost was claimed as a qualified expenditure (including materials transformed, property acquired under an arm's-length SR&ED contract, or depreciable capital property and Shared-Use Equipment acquired after December 15, 2024) is sold or converted to commercial use within 20 taxation years, the taxpayer must add back the recaptured ITC to its Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion6. Recapture is calculated on the lesser of the original qualified expenditure (or ITC earned) and the proceeds of disposition (for arm's-length sales) or fair market value (FMV) at conversion (for commercial conversions or non-arm's-length sales)6. Under paragraphs 127(27)(e) and (f), if a transformed material is incorporated into another property and cannot be physically separated from it, the proceeds of disposition or FMV of the entire containing property must be used to compute recapture6. Any ITC recaptured in a taxation year is added back to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2)23. Under current law, selling or licensing intellectual property (IP) generated during an SR&ED project does not trigger ITC recapture6.
3.5 Overhead, Cloud Computing, SaaS and Software Subscriptions

Claimants electing the Traditional Method (Line 162 of Form T661) may claim actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Line 36016. Under paragraph 2900(2)(c) and subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, every claimed overhead expenditure (or portion thereof) must satisfy two mandatory tests established in Tax Court jurisprudence (Ergorecherche et Conseils Inc. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1710; Data Kinetics Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1877; Quantetics Corporation v. The Queen, 2000 DTC 2177)16:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must proceed directly—without an intervening step or intermediary—and have a direct linkage to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED16.
The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure (or specific portion) would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred16.

body.text: Under the Traditional Method, items that generally pass both tests include incremental administrative/clerical salaries (HR, accounting, purchasing) directly aiding ongoing SR&ED, the employer's share of payroll benefits for hands-on SR&ED staff, utilities that vary directly with SR&ED equipment usage, maintenance and repairs of SR&ED premises and equipment, technological training and testing travel within Canada, long-distance phone charges directly tied to SR&ED, clinical study volunteer fees, and active-project waste disposal16. Items that fail the tests or are disallowed include fixed monthly telephone, mobile, and internet fees, fixed-cost maintenance contracts, general facility upkeep (hallways, lawn care, snow removal), recruiting/headhunter fees, post-project scrap disposal, and prescribed expenditures under Regulation 2902 (such as SR&ED claim preparation fees, conference attendance fees, and interest expenses)16.
Audit Treatment of Cloud Computing and Software Subscriptions

Cloud simulation subscriptions, CAD licences, and cloud computing capacity subscriptions are not qualified SR&ED expenditures15. Because they are not tangible physical substances, they do not qualify under the Materials for SR&ED Policy, nor are they SR&ED contracts performed on the claimant's behalf15. Under the Proxy Method, all overhead and indirect expenses are already represented by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Regulation 2900(4)), meaning cloud computing and software subscriptions cannot be claimed separately on Form T66115. Instead, they are deducted as ordinary business expenses under paragraph 18(1)(a) of the Income Tax Act15.

However, following the enactment of Bill C-15, software and AI businesses that purchase their own GPU servers, high-performance computing equipment, or specialized testing hardware—or purchase computers and software outright as depreciable property—after December 15, 2024 can claim those capital acquisitions as restored SR&ED capital expenditures (Line 390) if used 90% or more (ASA) for SR&ED in Canada, or as Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504) if used primarily (more than 50%) for SR&ED15. (For non-SR&ED tax depreciation, purchased application software falls into CCA Class 12 [100%] and systems software and computer hardware fall into CCA Class 50 [55% standard rate, with a 100% first-year accelerated deduction under Bill C-15 for property acquired after April 15, 2024 and available for use before 2027, and suspension of the half-year rule at three times the normal first-year amount for property acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030], though any property claimed on Form T661 Line 390 cannot also be depreciated via CCA on Schedule T2SCH84.)
3.6 Restored Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) and Equipment Leases (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014 and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures and equipment lease costs were excluded from the federal SR&ED program4. Bill C-15 restored three distinct pathways for claiming equipment and capital assets acquired or leased after December 15, 2024, governed by the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), and SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026)1.
1. All-or-Substantially-All (ASA) Capital Property (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Line 390 and Part 6B of Form T661)

To claim 100% of the capital cost of an owned asset on Line 390 of Form T661 (under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) for Traditional or subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III) for Proxy), the property must be depreciable property (subsection 13(21)) acquired and available for use (subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 202417. At the time of acquisition, the claimant must intend that the property will be used all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada, or that all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value will be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada17.

Land, leasehold interests in land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings (other than prescribed special-purpose buildings under Regulation 2903) are excluded1. Used equipment is restricted unless refurbished by the vendor prior to purchase to a state equivalent to new (if refurbished by the claimant after purchase, only the refurbishment cost qualifies)26. Under the Proxy Method, General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF—desks, chairs, lamps, filing cabinets, bookshelves, photocopiers, fax machines, telephones, cell phones, and calculators; note that computers, hardware, software, and ancillary equipment are not GPOEF) is excluded1. Qualifying ASA capital property enters the Section 37 deductible pool at 100% (replacing CCA on Schedule T2SCH8) and earns Section 127 ITCs (at 35% for CCPCs and ECPCs within their expenditure limit, of which 40% is refundable in cash)5.
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9), Regulation 2900(11), Line 504 and Part 6C of Form T661)

When a claimant acquires new depreciable equipment after December 15, 2024 that is used for both SR&ED and commercial operations—such that it does not meet the 90% lifecycle ASA test, is not GPOEF, and is not a Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under Regulation 2900(11) (which excludes buildings, commercial plant/line commissioning assets under paragraph 2900(11)(c), and property intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes over its useful life under paragraph 2900(11)(d))—the asset may qualify as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T66117:

items: First-Term SUE: If the new equipment is actually used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) of its actual operating time (excluding idle time) for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period—which starts when the property is acquired and available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time—25% (1/4) of the capital cost of the equipment (excluding borrowed money costs and adjusted for NAL costs under subsection 127(11.6)) is deemed to be a Section 127 qualified expenditure (Box 792 in Part 6C of Form T661)17.

Second-Term SUE: If the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE and continues to be used primarily (more than 50%) of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada during the Second Period—which starts when the equipment was acquired and available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time—an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost is deemed to be a Section 127 qualified expenditure17.

body.text: Across both terms, up to 50% (25% + 25%) of the capital cost of SUE earns Section 127 ITCs27. Unlike ASA capital property (Line 390), the capital cost of SUE does not enter the Section 37 deduction pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the cost under regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and any SUE ITC claimed or refunded reduces the UCC of the CCA class in the subsequent taxation year17. SUE ITC recapture is triggered if the property is sold or if all or substantially all of the property is converted to commercial use (i.e., SR&ED use becomes merely incidental), calculated on the lesser of the SUE ITC obtained and the ITC rate applied to 25% or 50% of the proceeds of disposition or FMV6.
3. Restored Equipment Lease Expenditures (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) and (B)(I)/(VI), Lines 350 and 355 of Form T661)

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 for the leasing of equipment (and structures, but not buildings other than Regulation 2903 special-purpose buildings; under the Traditional Method, lease of land is also allowable if ASA or directly attributable) qualify as current SR&ED expenditures1. For any taxation year that straddles December 16, 2024, the SR&ED operating-time percentage is measured over the total operating time of the equipment after December 15, 20241:

items: ASA Leased Equipment (90% or More SR&ED Operating Time): Under both the Traditional Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)) and the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), 100% of the lease cost incurred after December 15, 2024 is claimed on Line 350 of Form T661 (excluding GPOEF under the Proxy Method)1.

Primarily Used Leased Equipment (More than 50% and Less than 90% SR&ED Operating Time): Under the Proxy Method (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), 50% of the lease cost (excluding GPOEF) is claimed on Line 355 of Form T661, while equipment used 50% or less earns 0%1. body.text: 4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Post-Bill C-15 Alignment
4.1 The Federal-Provincial Assistance Grind (Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(18))

Across Canada, nine provinces and one territory (Yukon) offer subnational R&D tax credits that stack onto the federal SR&ED program11. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (as well as direct grants like NRC IRAP) are legally classified as "government assistance"4. Consequently, provincial R&D tax credits earned in a taxation year reduce—dollar for dollar—both the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (Line 513 of Form T661) before the federal 35% or 15% ITC rate is applied3. Claimants may waive or renounce certain provincial credits (such as Ontario's OITC or ORDTC, or BC, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, or Nova Scotia credits) within statutory deadlines if desired45.

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, a clear distinction emerged between "Follower" provinces (most notably British Columbia, which expressly aligned with the federal $6 million limit, ECPC eligibility, $15M–$75M phase-out, and restored capital expenditures) and "Holdout" or independently structured jurisdictions (such as Ontario, Alberta, Québec, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan, each of which maintains its own statutory thresholds, expenditure definitions, or incremental architectures)11.

body.text: 4.2 Detailed Provincial Deep Dives and Stacking Calculations
1. Ontario: OITC, ORDTC and OBRITC Stacking Mechanics

Ontario operates three separate R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA as part of the harmonized T2 corporate income tax return45. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566) provides an 8% fully refundable credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (shared among associated corporations; Ontario has not adopted the federal $6,000,000 cap, and current CRA guidance does not confirm that restored federal capital expenditures have been added to the OITC base, though another industry blog notes potential OITC inclusion)11. The $3 million OITC limit is reduced by two statutory grinds across the associated group: it phases out when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when prior-year specified paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,00011.

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit on all eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures with no expenditure cap25. Crucially, the Government of Ontario's official ORDTC page confirms that eligible ORDTC expenditures include 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (while excluding capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 and before December 16, 2024)25. In computing the ORDTC base on Schedule 508, the corporation must first subtract the current-year OITC entitlement because the OITC is a form of government assistance that reduces eligible expenditures for the ORDTC25. Both the OITC and the ORDTC (unless waived under subsection 96(14) or subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario)) then reduce the federal qualified expenditure pool on Line 513 of Form T66145. (Note that Ontario also offers the non-SR&ED Ontario Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit [OIDMTC] at 40% for in-house products and 35% for fee-for-service products45.)

To illustrate the exact statutory stacking calculation in Ontario (58), consider an Ontario CCPC (below the $500K taxable income and $15M/$25M capital phase-outs) that incurs $400,000 in direct Ontario SR&ED salaries, elects the Proxy Method (generating $220,000 in 55% PPA), and pays $150,000 to an arm's-length Ontario contractor (80% qualified = $120,000), yielding total pre-assistance qualified expenditures of $740,00058:

items: OITC (Schedule 566): 8% × $740,000 = $59,200 (fully refundable cash)58.
ORDTC (Schedule 508): Base is reduced by OITC ($740,000 − $59,200 = $680,800). ORDTC = 3.5% × $680,800 = $23,828 (non-refundable credit against Ontario corporate tax)58.

Federal SR&ED ITC (Schedule T2SCH31): Federal qualified expenditures are reduced by both Ontario credits ($740,000 − $59,200 − $23,828 = $656,972). Federal enhanced ITC = 35% × $656,972 = $229,940 (fully refundable cash)58.
Combined Recovery: Total federal and Ontario credits equal $59,200 + $23,828 + $229,940 = $312,96858.

body.text: 2. Québec: The CRIC Overhaul (Effective for Tax Years Beginning After March 25, 2025)

In its 2025–2026 Budget (tabled March 25, 2025, Information Bulletin 2025-6), the Government of Québec enacted a comprehensive structural consolidation of its innovation tax system20. For taxation years (and partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished eight legacy measures—specifically the Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D) (Form RD-1029.7), the Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.6), the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research (Form RD-1029.8.16.1), the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium (Form RD-1029.8.9.03; transitional eligible fee balances can be claimed up to December 31, 2029), the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, and the industrial design component of the Tax Credit for In-House Design Activities—and replaced them with the single Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR18.

Under the CRIC, any eligible corporation with an establishment in Québec earns a fully refundable tax credit equal to 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the applicable exclusion threshold (allocated among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN), and 20% on all qualified expenditures over that $1,000,000 bracket18. In addition to R&D (where the scientific definition remains harmonized with federal subsection 248(1) and the CRA conducts the scientific review), the CRIC covers pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with R&D work: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies to meet regulatory requirements for obtaining initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation (including quality control activities related solely to implementing a quality control system required for initial certification), and (2) product design, including developing form, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials11.

Qualified expenditures under the CRIC comprise 100% of employee salaries and wages for eligible work in Québec, 50% of payments to subcontractors for contracts carried out in Québec, 50% of payments to eligible public research centres, research consortia, or university entities, and 100% of property acquisition costs (capital equipment) used in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec (excluding land and buildings; property claimed under CRIC cannot also be claimed under the Québec Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation [C3i, Form CO-1029.8.36.II], which pays 15%, 20%, or 25% depending on regional economic vitality)18. The CRIC exclusion threshold is the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec personal income tax basic personal amount ($18,571 in 2025) for each eligible employee, prorated by the percentage of time each employee spends on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities18.
3. Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) Two-Step Incremental Mechanics

Administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) under Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (Information Circular IEG-1) and claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29, Rev. 2026-06) alongside Form AT4970 (Listing of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Claimed in Alberta), the IEG is an incremental refundable tax credit worth up to 20% on up to $4,000,000 of annual Alberta SR&ED spending (maximum $800,000 grant per year, phasing out for prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000)3.

The IEG operates via a two-tier calculation against the corporation's Base Amount (Line 118 of Form AT29), which equals the corporation's average eligible Alberta R&D expenditures over the two immediately preceding taxation years59. In Part I (Line 110), every dollar of eligible Alberta expenditure up to the $4M limit earns an 8% base payment; in Part II (Line 112), every dollar of eligible Alberta expenditure that exceeds the 2-year Base Amount (up to the $4M limit) earns an additional 12% incremental payment, creating a combined 20% refundable rate (8% + 12%) on incremental R&D spending above the two-year average11. For example, if an Alberta corporation has a two-year average Base Amount of $1.5M and incurs $3.0M in current-year eligible Alberta expenditures, the first $1.5M earns 8% ($120,000) and the $1.5M incremental slice earns 20% ($300,000), for a total refundable IEG of $420,00091.

On June 30, 2026, Alberta published updated IEG guidance and revised Form AT29 (Rev. 2026-06) confirming that for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, the IEG uses the federal amount of current SR&ED expenditures reported on Line 557 of federal Form T661 (rather than Line 559), meaning Alberta did not adopt the federal $6 million limit or restored federal capital expenditures11. In Step 1 of Form AT29, the corporation calculates its preliminary IEG (including the 55% Alberta proxy amount on Line 009) before deducting the IEG on federal Form T661; in Step 2, that IEG is deducted as provincial government assistance on Line 513 of federal Form T661 to reduce the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool75.
5. Federal Direct R&D Grants, Ecosystem Programs and IP Box Regimes
5.1 NRC Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) and Stacking Mechanics

Established in 1962 and administered by the National Research Council of Canada (NRC) through a network of approximately 275 Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) across 128 offices, NRC IRAP is Canada's flagship direct, non-repayable R&D contribution program for incorporated, for-profit Canadian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent (FTE) employees98.
As of 2026, NRC IRAP operates four main funding streams alongside its Youth Employment Program (YEP) sub-stream98:

items: Core IRAP: Supports technical R&D projects across all sectors (with ICT/software representing 29% of clients, alongside life sciences, advanced manufacturing, clean tech, and agri-tech)98. Typical first-time awards range from $75,000 to $200,000 (overall median award of $75,000; pilot projects under $50,000 average ~9 days processing time; major projects can reach up to a $10,000,000 ceiling)98.

NRC IRAP Clean Technology Stream (Absorbed SDTC Mandate): Formed in June 2024 when NRC IRAP absorbed the programming of Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC)98. Supports SMEs developing, demonstrating, and commercializing clean technology solutions with a validated proof of concept (Technology Readiness Level [TRL] 5 or higher) and measurable environmental benefits (such as GHG emission reductions in tonnes per year)98. Typical awards range from $100,000 to $1,000,000+, with a 2025 median award of $983,700 (middle 50% between $469,100 and $2.05M across 103 recipients)98.

Defence Industry Assist (DI Assist): Launched in January 2026 with $244.2 million in dedicated funding for dual-use technologies in cybersecurity, autonomous systems, and advanced materials (typical awards of $100,000 to $500,000)98.

AI Assist: A $100 million five-year initiative delivered through the ITA network to support SMEs building and deploying Generative AI (GenAI), Deep Neural Networks (DNN), and Deep Learning (DL) solutions98.

body.text: IRAP Reimbursement Rates and SR&ED Stacking Interaction

NRC IRAP reimburses up to 80% of eligible internal technical employee salary costs and up to 50% of arm's-length subcontractor costs directly required for the R&D project, subject to a 75% total government assistance cap across all federal, provincial, and municipal programs98. Unlike SR&ED (which is claimed retrospectively up to 18 months after the fiscal year-end), IRAP is strictly prospective: an applicant must contact NRC IRAP (1-877-994-4727), be assigned an ITA, co-develop a formal proposal, and sign a contribution agreement before starting work98.

When a company stacks NRC IRAP and federal SR&ED on the same project, the IRAP grant is included in taxable income and constitutes government assistance under ITA paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18), reducing the SR&ED expenditure base dollar-for-dollar4. However, under the Proxy Method (Income Tax Regulations subsection 2900(4)), the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated on the full eligible direct SR&ED salary base before deducting the IRAP grant, and the claimant then claims SR&ED on the remaining un-reimbursed salary plus the full 55% PPA, allowing combined IRAP and SR&ED funding to offset more than 60% to 75% of total R&D project costs3.

body.text: 5.3 Intellectual Property (IP) and Patent Box Regimes in Canada
1. Federal Patent Box Consultation and OECD BEPS Action 5 Nexus Framework

Following nearly $100 million in federal IP investments in Budget 2022 (including ElevateIP and IP Assist and the 2023 Strategic Intellectual Property Program Review), the Department of Finance Canada conducted a formal public consultation from January 31, 2024 to April 15, 2024 on creating a federal Patent Box regime111. As documented in the Department of Finance consultation paper, Canadian businesses face a persistent net balance-of-payments deficit in charges for the use of IP—reaching $8.078 billion USD in 2021, compared to a G7 average net surplus of $19.839 billion USD112. The consultation paper confirmed that any federal Canadian patent box must comply with the OECD BEPS Action 5 "Nexus Approach" (and OECD transfer pricing DEMPE principles—Development, Enhancement, Maintenance, Protection, and Exploitation), which restricts preferential IP tax rates to three categories of qualifying IP assets—(1) patents defined broadly (including utility models, plants and genetic material, orphan drug designations, and extensions of patent protection), (2) copyrighted software, and (3) other non-obvious, useful, and novel IP assets certified as substantially similar (available only to SMEs below a certain size)—and limits eligible IP income to the extent that the taxpayer itself incurred the qualifying R&D expenditures that gave rise to the IP income112. While a federal patent box has not yet been enacted into the Income Tax Act as of November 2026, two Canadian provinces—Québec and Saskatchewan—operate active subnational patent box regimes114.
2. Québec's Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI / DICI)

Introduced in March 2020 (replacing an earlier 2016 deduction) and applicable to taxation years beginning after December 31, 2020 (S.Q. 2021, c. 14, ss. 76 and 198), Québec's Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI)—claimed on Form CO-737.18.CI (2025-03)—reduces the Québec provincial corporate income tax rate from the general rate of 11.5% down to an effective rate of 2% (a 9.5 percentage point reduction, bringing the combined federal-Québec corporate tax rate down from 26.5% to 17%) on the qualified portion of income derived from commercializing a qualified IP asset116.

A qualified IP asset under the IDCI must be incorporeal property resulting from R&D activities carried out in whole or in part in Québec that significantly contributed to its creation, development, or improvement, consisting of: (1) an invention protected by a patent or certificate of supplementary protection; (2) software protected by copyright; or (3) a plant variety protected by a plant breeder's rights certificate116. Qualified gross income must be reasonably attributable to a Québec establishment and come from royalties, the sale or lease of property incorporating the IP asset, services intrinsically related to the IP asset, or judicial damages relating to the asset (capital gains from the sale of IP rights are excluded)116.
On Form CO-737.18.CI, the IDCI deduction is determined using variables A through G116:
IDCI = [(A × B ÷ C) − D] × (E ÷ F) × G

where A is net income for tax purposes; B is gross income from commercializing the qualified IP asset; C is total gross income; D is the estimate of routine profit not attributable to the IP asset; E / F (Québec Nexus Ratio) is the ratio of qualified R&D expenditures related to the IP asset and linked to Québec (E) to overall R&D expenditures related to the IP asset (F), calculated on a cumulative moving-average basis over the current taxation year and the 6 preceding taxation years (and not reduced by the CRIC exclusion threshold); and G is the rate conversion factor (11.5% − 2%) / 11.5% = 82.6% (reported as 0.826 in simplified form)115. The IDCI is cumulative with federal SR&ED ITCs and the Québec CRIC117.
3. Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII)

Saskatchewan's Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII) reduces the Saskatchewan provincial corporate income tax rate to 6% for a period of 10 years on taxable income derived from the commercialization of eligible IP, which can be extended to 15 years if the related R&D is conducted in Saskatchewan114.
