Section B totals allowable SR&ED expenditures (including restored ASA equipment leases on Line 350, 50% Proxy primarily used leases on Line 355, Traditional overhead on Line 360, and restored ASA capital property on Line 390). Section C computes the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures16.

Computes the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool: adds the 55% PPA (Line 502), adds 25% First-Term / 25% Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment (Line 504), includes 80% of arm's-length contracts and third-party payments, and deducts provincial/federal assistance (Line 513)16.
Applies the Regulation 2900(7) caps for specified employees (75% or 2.5 × YMPE × days/365), multiplies by 55%, and tests against the Regulation 2900(6) Overall Cap14.
Part 6 (All project costs) Part 6B (ASA Capital Property) Part 6C / Box 792 (Shared-Use Equipment)

Part 6 allocates costs across all claimed projects70. Part 6B details post-Dec 15, 2024 ASA capital property122. Part 6C (Box 792) lists the 20 most expensive post-Dec 15, 2024 SUE properties at 25% of capital cost17.

Part 9 requires prescribed information for every claim preparer that accepted consideration to prepare or assist with the claim. Missing, incomplete, or inaccurate Part 9 information triggers a $1,000 joint-and-several penalty under ITA subsection 162(5.1), though it does not disallow the SR&ED claim itself9.

body.text: 6.2 Statutory Reporting Deadlines and the Non-Extension Rule (Subsections 37(11), 37(12), 127(9)(m) and 220(2.2))

Under subsection 37(11) (for the Section 37 expenditure deduction) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for the Section 127 ITC), a claimant's statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date (section 150) for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred4:

items: Corporations (Paragraph 150(1)(a)): Because a T2 corporate return is due 6 months after the end of the taxation year, the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, for a December 31, 2024 year-end, the deadline is June 30, 2026; for a December 31, 2025 year-end, the deadline is June 30, 2027)4.

Individuals (Sole Proprietorships): Because a self-employed individual's T1 return is due June 15 of the following calendar year, the SR&ED reporting deadline (Form T661 and Form T2038(IND)) is 12 months after the T1 filing due date (17.5 months after the December 31 year-end, falling in mid-June of the second following year)70.
Trusts: The SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the trust income tax return (T3) filing due date70.

Partnerships: Where a partnership files a Partnership Information Return (Form T5013), the partnership's Form T661 must be filed no later than 12 months after the earliest partner's filing due date (the earliest member's SR&ED reporting deadline) to ensure all members can claim their allocated ITCs, and each member must file its own Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) by its own respective reporting deadline70.

body.text: Under subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12), if a taxpayer fails to file Form T661 containing the prescribed information for an expenditure on or before the reporting deadline, no deduction may be made under subsection 37(1) and the expenditure is deemed not to be an expenditure on or in respect of SR&ED9. If Form T661 is filed on time, but Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) is filed after the reporting deadline, the claimant may still include the allowable expenditures in the Section 37 deductible pool, but is not entitled to earn any Section 127 ITC on those expenditures70. Under subsection 220(2.2), there is no statutory mechanism or ministerial discretion to extend the SR&ED reporting deadline; taxpayer relief under subsection 220(3.1) applies only to penalties and interest, and no new projects or substitute expenditures can be added after the 18-month deadline passes4. The CRA recommends filing at least 90 days before the 18-month deadline so any missing prescribed fields can be supplied before the window closes4. Under paragraph 230(4)(b), all supporting books and records must be retained for 6 years from the end of the last taxation year to which the records relate4.
6.3 The Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026 — Form T1322)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched its optional Pre-Claim Approval Process, allowing eligible businesses to obtain an upfront technical determination of whether planned projects meet the statutory definition of SR&ED before beginning work or incurring costs3. To qualify, the applicant must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a partnership operating in Canada that is in good standing with the CRA and has less than $25,000,000 in annual gross business income9. A business may request pre-claim approval for up to 3 projects per application, and each project must represent new work (not yet started or only recently begun) that has not been claimed in a previous taxation year and is not under objection or litigation9.
The Pre-Claim Approval workflow proceeds in four steps9:

items: Request a Case Number: The business submits a short web form with its contact name, legal name, and Business Number; the CRA contacts existing claimants in good standing within 2 business days via My Business Account and other applicants within 5 business days by phone9.

Submit Form T1322 in My Business Account: The business completes Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development [SR&ED] pre-claim approval), entering the case number on Line 016 and addressing three core technical prompts per project: (a) the scientific or technological uncertainty (maximum 500 words); (b) the due diligence completed to confirm the uncertainty cannot be resolved using existing knowledge (maximum 700 words); and (c) the planned systematic investigation work over the approval period of up to 3 years (maximum 900 words)9.

Meet with a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA): Within approximately 4 weeks of submitting the application, the CRA schedules a 2- to 5-hour meeting with an assigned RTA (mandatory for new claimants; optional at the RTA's request for existing claimants in good standing)9.

Receive Written Determination Within 8 Weeks: Within 8 weeks of receiving a complete application, the CRA issues a Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report confirming whether pre-claim approval is granted (valid for up to 3 years)9.

body.text: Pre-claim approval confirms technical project eligibility rather than final expenditure amounts; the business must still file Form T661 (reporting the case number on Lines 212 and 214) after each taxation year3. However, if a refundable SR&ED claim containing only pre-approved projects is selected for an expenditure review, the CRA's processing service standard is cut in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days9. There is no appeal or formal objection process if pre-claim approval is not granted, though the business may either submit a revised pre-claim application (if material changes are made) or proceed with the work and file a standard post-year-end Form T661 claim9.
6.4 CRA Review Service Standards, Audit Procedures, Penalties and Appeals
1. CRA Service Standards and Review Roles

Once a complete SR&ED claim is received, the CRA either accepts the claim as filed or selects it for review (approximately 20% of claims are reviewed, and once selected, a claim cannot be withdrawn)62:

items: 60 Calendar Days: Service standard for claims accepted as filed without a review124.
90 Calendar Days: Service standard for refundable claims selected for review where every project in the claim received Pre-Claim Approval9.

180 Calendar Days: Standard service timeline for refundable claims selected for review where any project lacks pre-claim approval or differs materially from what was approved35. (Note: Older CRA targets of 120 days for refundable claims and 365 days for non-refundable claims130 have been updated to the 60 / 90 / 180 calendar-day framework, with non-refundable claims currently carrying no formal service standard126.)

body.text: During a review, the Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) evaluates technical eligibility under the Claim Review Manual (CRM) for RTAs and prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, while the Financial Reviewer (FR) (reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM]) examines financial ledgers, payroll, time sheets, contracts, and equipment logs under the Financial Claim Review Manual to prepare the Financial Review Report (FRR) (formerly the T20 report)121.
2. Proposal Letters (30 Days), Administrative Second Review (Form RC532) and Formal Appeals

When reviewers propose adjustments, the CRA issues a Proposal Package containing the eligibility report, proposed financial adjustments, and any penalty proposals, giving the claimant 30 calendar days to submit written representations or additional supporting evidence126. If concerns remain regarding how the review was conducted, the CRA provides a three-step dispute resolution process: (1) speak with the RTA or FR; (2) escalate to the RTM or FRM; and (3) before the reviewers close the file (notifying them before the 30-day proposal window expires), submit Form RC532 to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre to request an Administrative Second Review126. Conducted by a local SR&ED Assistant Director, the Administrative Second Review examines whether due process was provided and CRA policy was properly followed, rather than conducting a de novo scientific audit126.

Requesting an Administrative Second Review does not pause the 90-day statutory objection clock126. Once the CRA issues a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, a corporation has strictly 90 calendar days from the date on the notice (paragraph 165(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act) to file a Notice of Objection online via My Business Account or on Form T400A addressed to the Chief of Appeals (individuals have the later of 90 days from the notice or 1 year after their T1 filing-due date under paragraph 165(1)(a); missed objection deadlines may be extended by application within 1 year under subsection 166.1(1))9. Corporations that are "Large Corporations" (over $10,000,000 in taxable capital employed in Canada, including related corporations) must reasonably describe each issue, state the exact dollar relief sought, provide full facts and legal grounds, and pay 50% of the disputed amount while the objection is pending126.

If the CRA Appeals Officer issues a Notice of Confirmation (or if 90 days pass after filing an income tax objection without a CRA decision under paragraph 169(1)(b)), the taxpayer may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada within 90 days of the confirmation notice (missed appeal deadlines may be extended within 1 year under section 167)9. Appeals where the disputed federal tax and penalties are $25,000 or less per taxation year (or disputed loss is $50,000 or less) may elect the Informal Procedure (subsection 18(1) of the Tax Court of Canada Act, $0 filing fee); all other appeals proceed under the General Procedure (Form 21(1)(a), with Registry filing fees of $250 for Class A [under $50K], $400 for Class B [$50K to under $150K], or $550 for Class C [$150K or more])126. Final judgments of the Tax Court of Canada may be appealed to the Federal Court of Appeal within 30 days (excluding July and August)126.
3. Statutory Penalties Applicable to SR&ED Claims

cells: Claim Preparer Information Penalty (Claimant and Claim Preparer jointly and severally)9

$1,000 per claim where prescribed claim preparer identity or billing arrangement details in Part 9 of Form T661 are missing, incomplete, or false (subject to a due-diligence defence for the preparer)9.

Greater of $100 and 50% of the understated tax and/or 50% of the excess refundable SR&ED ITC claimed under subsection 127.1(1) (paragraph 163(2)(d)), where a false statement or omission is made knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence. Burden of proof rests on the Minister under subsection 163(3)9.

Applies to advisers/preparers who make or participate in false statements knowingly or via culpable conduct. Preparer Penalty (163.2(4)–(5)): Greater of $1,000 and the lesser of (a) the client's 163(2) penalty and (b) $100,000 plus 100% of the preparer's gross compensation9.

Obtaining or claiming an SR&ED refund/credit via false or deceptive statements: on summary conviction, a fine of 50% to 200% of the excess credit and up to 2 years' imprisonment; on indictment, a fine of 100% to 200% and up to 5 years' imprisonment9.

body.text: 7. Foundational and Contemporary Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence

Canadian SR&ED tax administration is anchored in judicial precedent13. Because subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act sets out broad statutory principles, decisions of the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) establish the binding legal tests for technological uncertainty, systematic investigation, contemporaneous documentation, and overhead eligibility13.

cells: Definition of Systematic Investigation: Held that SR&ED requires a systematic investigation or search carried out by means of trained, systematic observation, measurement, and experiment—not unmeasured shop-floor trial-and-error136.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen , 98 DTC 183912

The Foundational 5-Question SR&ED Test: Allowed hydraulic modelling claims; articulated the five canonical criteria for SR&ED, recognized system uncertainty, distinguished routine engineering, and confirmed that failed hypotheses still advance technological knowledge12.
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen , 99 DTC 5087 (rev'g 97 DTC 99)141

Evidentiary Burden & Repeatability: Held that once a trial judge concludes that testing occurred and produced a technological advancement, a rebuttable inference arises that the work met SR&ED criteria; requiring documentary proof of exact test repeatability is an error of law141.

Appellate Adoption of Northwest Hydraulic: Formally adopted and reiterated Justice Bowman's five-question framework from Northwest Hydraulic as the governing standard at the Federal Court of Appeal143.
Zeuter Development Corporation v. The Queen , 2006 TCC 597138
Reliance on Sass Manufacturing & Systematic Investigation: Applied the Sass Manufacturing and Northwest Hydraulic principles regarding systematic investigation138.
Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen , 2011 TCC 261 (aff'd 2011 FCA 355)144

Proving Failure of Standard Practice: Held that unless work is "new to the world," the taxpayer must lead objective evidence showing how existing methods and standard practices failed to achieve the objective; warned against relying on narrow Statements of Agreed Facts or lay opinion144.
6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2014/2015 TCC)143

Contemporaneous Documentation Not Sine Qua Non: Held that contemporaneous documentation is not an absolute legal condition sine qua non for allowing an SR&ED claim if credible evidence proves the statutory criteria, and that projects must be evaluated globally over the year rather than isolating individual tests143.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen , 2017 TCC 6136

Personnel Qualifications & Quantitative Measurement: Upheld denial of a motorized hydraulic theatre fire-curtain project as routine engineering; highlighted the absence of trained engineering staff, lack of explicit hypotheses, and failure to measure curtain descent duration during testing136.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada , 2021 FCA 8813

Binding Authority of the "Scientific Method": Rejected the taxpayer's argument that the "scientific method" is not required because the phrase does not appear in subsection 248(1); reaffirmed that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria are the appropriate judicial interpretation of s. 248(1)13.
Logix Data Products Inc. v. The Queen , 2021 TCC 3639

Objective vs. Subjective Uncertainty Standard: Denied solar shingle claim; held that "technological uncertainty" is strictly an objective standard measured against competent professionals in the relevant industry—not the subjective knowledge gap of non-engineers39.
Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen , 2022 TCC 29147

Mapping the "Why" and "How" & Flawed CRA Reviews: Mapped Northwest Hydraulic Questions 1 & 4 to the "Why" and Questions 2, 3 & 5 to the "How"; allowed 4 of 6 air-contaminant sampling projects; faulted the CRA for relying on general, undocumented Google searches147.

CRA Guidelines Cannot Override Appellate Precedent: Dismissed appeal by SR&ED consulting firm regarding its web-based "Project Tracking System"; held that the CRA's 2021 revised guidelines do not dilute the Northwest Hydraulic / Kam-Press scientific method discipline, and that vague records failed to show logical progression13.
Dave's Diesel Inc. (June 2022 TCC), JEC Distributors Inc. (Dec 2022 TCC) & Paveit Construction Inc. (Sept 2025 TCC)39

Decisive Weight of Independent Expert Witnesses: Dismissed taxpayer appeals where claimants failed to lead independent expert evidence to prove that uncertainties could not be resolved by routine engineering accessible to competent professionals in the field39.

Traditional Overhead Tests (Reg. 2900(2)(c)): Established the strict "directly related" (no intervening step) and "incremental" (but-for causation) requirements for claiming overhead under the Traditional Method65.

body.text: 7.1 Deep Legal Analysis of Controlling Precedents
1. Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839) and the Five-Question Test

Decided by Justice Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in May 1998, Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen remains the foundational judicial decision in Canadian SR&ED law12. The appellant carried on a specialized hydraulic engineering practice and claimed SR&ED tax incentives for 17 river and hydraulic engineering modelling projects conducted between 1983 and 199412. Overturning the Minister's disallowance, Justice Bowman articulated the five exact questions that Canadian courts apply to determine whether work qualifies as SR&ED12:

items: Is there a technical risk or uncertainty? Justice Bowman specified that this uncertainty must be one that cannot be removed by "routine engineering or standard procedures," defining routine engineering as "those techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field"12. If the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures, there is no technological uncertainty, though genuine system uncertainty can arise even where individual components are well understood39.
Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?12

Did the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses?12

Did the process result in a technological advance, that is to say an advancement in the general understanding? Crucially, the rejection of a hypothesis after systematic testing is itself a technological advancement because proving that an approach fails advances technological knowledge3.
Did the taxpayer keep a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests and results as the work progressed?12

body.text: 2. Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72)

Both shortly before and after the CRA's August 2021 release of its simplified "Why" and "How" eligibility guidelines (which removed the explicit phrase "scientific method" from administrative web pages)37, taxpayers argued before the Federal Court of Appeal that the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion—adherence to the total discipline of the scientific method—was not a statutory requirement under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act13. In both Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72, written by Justice Donald Rennie), the Federal Court of Appeal rejected this contention13. In National R&D, an SR&ED consulting firm claimed credits for its 2011 taxation year for developing a web-based, cross-platform, cross-browser "Project Tracking System"13. Justice Rennie held that administrative guidance published by the CRA is non-binding on the courts, which are governed by appellate precedent and the rules of statutory interpretation in Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada; that the Northwest Hydraulic criteria reflect Parliament's intended meaning in subsection 248(1); that the CRA's "How" requirement still mandates underlying rigour and discipline in the experimental process; and that the appellant's vague, unclear records failed to show a logical progression between experimental premises and results13.
3. Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen (2022 TCC 29)

In Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen (2022 TCC 29), the Tax Court of Canada directly bridged the CRA's 2021 "Why" and "How" guidelines with the five-question Northwest Hydraulic model147. The appellant conducted six projects in 2014 and 2015 involving air quality monitoring and sampling of airborne contaminants147. The Minister conceded that the appellant satisfied the "How" requirement (Questions 2, 3, and 5 of Northwest Hydraulic), but disallowed all six projects for allegedly failing the "Why" requirement (Questions 1 and 4—technological uncertainty and advancement)147. Allowing four of the six projects (while upholding the disallowance of two routine projects), the Tax Court established three important principles147:

items: Relationship Between the "How" and the "Why": The Court noted that it is unlikely a commercial taxpayer would conduct a costly systematic investigation satisfying the "How" unless the work were genuinely undertaken to resolve a technological uncertainty and achieve a technological advancement147.

Flawed CRA Literature Reviews: Under cross-examination, the CRA revealed that its conclusion that there was no technological advancement was based on a general Google search on air quality analyses, and the CRA could not recall or cite the specific sources consulted147.

Development of New Protocols for Complex Variables: Detecting and measuring an array of 52 airborne contaminants presented too many variables and unknowns where extraction data was not publicly available, requiring Airzone to develop entirely new protocols rather than applying routine analytical chemistry147.

body.text: 4. Evidentiary Standards: RIS-Christie, 6379249 Canada Inc., Joel Theatrical Rigging, Logix Data and Paveit Construction

Taken together, the remaining foundational cases establish a clear evidentiary roadmap for audit defence and Tax Court litigation. While the CRA's Form T661 checklist (Lines 270–282) emphasizes contemporaneous records, both the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 5087) and the Tax Court in 6379249 Canada Inc. and Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6) confirm that contemporaneous documentation is not a strict legal condition sine qua non136. However, where documentation is incomplete, the taxpayer must still prove through credible evidence that hypotheses were formulated and systematically measured—as illustrated in Joel Theatrical Rigging, where the working employees had no mechanical or hydraulic engineering diplomas, formulated no testable hypotheses, and failed to measure the descent duration of a hydraulic theatre fire curtain across trials136.

Finally, in Logix Data Products Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 36), the Tax Court emphasized that "the 'technological uncertainty' standard, however, is not subjective. If it were subjective, a grade school student trying to build a simple electric motor would meet the test"39. As reinforced in Dave's Diesel Inc. (June 2022 TCC), JEC Distributors Inc. (December 2022 TCC), and Paveit Construction Inc. (September 2025 TCC), the test for technological uncertainty is strictly an objective standard measured against competent professionals in the relevant field of science or technology—making the testimony of an impartial, independent expert witness a decisive factor in winning SR&ED appeals before the Tax Court of Canada39.
